planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring into cool, acidic, humus-rich soil beneath conifer canopy in partial to full shade; fool's huckleberry is a true deep-shade understory shrub of wet western hemlock and Sitka spruce forests and resents hot, dry, or alkaline sites.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring into cool, acidic, humus-rich soil beneath conifer canopy in partial to full shade, mimicking the deep litter and constant moisture of its native Olympic Peninsula hemlock-cedar forests. Menziesia ferruginea is a loosely branched, deciduous Ericaceae shrub with soft, rust-colored hairs on new twigs and foliage, bluish-green leaves that turn orange-red in fall, and small, nodding, urn-shaped flowers in dusty pink to coppery orange held in clusters along the stems each late spring. It is a slow, long-lived companion for rhododendron, salal, and huckleberry in a woodland planting and needs no fertilizer beyond an annual top-dressing of leaf mold or conifer duff to replicate forest floor conditions. The foliage and nectar are mildly toxic if ingested in quantity, so it is grown strictly as an ornamental or wildlife shrub rather than for any food use.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall along streambanks or seep edges in constantly moist, mossy, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this species comes from mist-drenched rock faces and nurse logs in Olympic Peninsula rainforest ravines and will not tolerate drying out.

directions: Plant divisions or container plants in fall along streambanks, seep edges, or shaded rock walls in constantly moist, mossy, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, reproducing the wet rock faces and nurse logs where it naturally grows in Olympic Peninsula rainforest ravines. Saxifraga mertensiana forms a loose rosette of round, coarsely toothed, kidney-shaped leaves on reddish stalks, sending up airy, branched sprays of small white flowers in spring that are frequently replaced by tiny bulblets instead of seed, allowing the plant to spread clonally down wet slopes. It is best tucked into a shaded rock garden, bog garden margin, or the base of a mossy log where runoff keeps the roots cool and wet through summer, and it resents any site that dries even briefly. Established plants need no feeding and benefit from a yearly topping of leaf litter or fine bark to hold moisture at the crown.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall into cool, wet, acidic duff in deep shade under conifers; Oregon goldthread spreads by thin golden rhizomes just under the moss layer and needs the same saturated, shaded conditions as its native coastal rainforest understory.

directions: Plant divisions in fall into cool, consistently wet, acidic duff in deep shade beneath hemlock or cedar, matching the moss-carpeted coastal conifer forest floor of the Olympic Peninsula and Oregon Coast Range where it grows wild. Coptis laciniata forms a low, glossy evergreen mat of deeply cut, fern-like, parsley-textured leaves threaded together by thin, bright gold rhizomes, with small white star-shaped flowers held on wiry stalks just above the foliage in spring. It is slow to establish but forms a dense, weed-suppressing carpet once rooted into moist humus, making it a choice groundcover for the darkest, wettest corner of a woodland garden where few other perennials thrive. Keep the crown shaded and never let the planting dry out, since this species comes from sites with near-constant rainfall or seepage and has little drought tolerance.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to light dappled sun; this fully double-flowered salmonberry selection is grown for its showy magenta-pink spring bloom and produces little to no fruit.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to light dappled sun, reproducing the damp forest-edge and streamside conditions of the wild Pacific Northwest salmonberry it was selected from. 'Olympic Double' bears dense clusters of fully double, rose-magenta flowers that smother the bare, cane-like stems from late winter into spring, far showier than the single five-petaled flowers of the wild species, though the extra petals largely replace the stamens so fruit set is sparse to none. Its cane growth and bristly, maple-like leaves are otherwise typical of salmonberry, suckering readily to form a loose thicket useful for a damp woodland edge, rain garden margin, or wildlife hedge where winter hummingbirds visit the early flowers. Prune out the oldest canes at the base every few years to keep the thicket from becoming congested and to encourage strong new flowering wood.
